questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for ovarian cancer has an episode of acute vomiting despite her scheduled prophylaxis. She is given an intravenous agent that is also prescribed for diabetic gastroparesis. Its antiemetic effect comes mainly from receptor blockade in the area postrema of the medulla. Which receptor is the principal target of this drug?

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide's main antiemetic action is D2 antagonism in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema).
explanation.whyCorrect: The drug described is metoclopramide, a D2 antagonist also used to speed gastric emptying in diabetic gastroparesis. Blocking D2 receptors in the area postrema inhibits stimulation of the vomiting center. It has added 5-HT3 antagonism, but its primary antiemetic action is through D2 blockade.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone act through anti-inflammatory effects, not through the area postrema receptor that metoclopramide blocks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine-1 receptors are present in the CTZ, but they are not the primary target of metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M1 blockade is how scopolamine treats vestibular nausea, not how metoclopramide works.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK1 receptors are blocked by aprepitant, which inhibits substance P binding.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man starting doxorubicin is prescribed granisetron for prophylaxis of chemotherapy-induced nausea. His physician explains that the drug acts at two sites: in the brainstem trigger zone and in the periphery. At which peripheral site does this drug act?

explanation.summary: 5-HT3 antagonists block 5-HT3 receptors both in the CTZ and on peripheral vagal nerve terminals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granisetron, like ondansetron and palonosetron, is a selective 5-HT3 antagonist. Chemotherapy irritates the GI tract, causing mucosal serotonin release that activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferent terminals. Blocking these peripheral receptors, along with central receptors in the CTZ, prevents nausea and vomiting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vestibular nausea is targeted by antimuscarinics such as scopolamine, not by 5-HT3 antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The adrenal medulla is not a site of 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parietal cells are not described as a site of antiemetic action for any agent in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Kupffer cells play no role in the antiemetic mechanism of 5-HT3 antagonists.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with lung cancer is scheduled to start cisplatin. Her oncologist plans to give aprepitant. She asks whether she can keep the pills at home and take one only if she starts to feel sick. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is reserved for nausea caused by motion sickness

choices.label: B
choices.text: It must be given before the infusion to prevent symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: It must be given only with meals to be absorbed

choices.label: D
choices.text: It should be used only once all other agents fail

choices.label: E
choices.text: It works best when taken only after vomiting has already begun

explanation.summary: Because aprepitant prevents substance P from binding NK1 receptors, it is given as pre-treatment about 30 minutes before chemotherapy, not as needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aprepitant blocks NK1 receptors to inhibit binding of substance P. Because of this mechanism it is not effective on an as-needed basis. It is used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and is given about 30 minutes before the chemotherapy infusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Motion sickness is treated with antimuscarinics such as scopolamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meal timing is not the issue the brick raises; the key point is timing relative to the chemotherapy infusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Breakthrough use after other agents fail describes the role of D2 antagonists, not aprepitant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aprepitant is not effective on an as-needed basis; it is given as pre-treatment, not after symptoms start.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with testicular cancer will begin a regimen whose chemotherapeutic agent causes emesis in more than 90% of patients. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial antiemetic plan for the day of infusion?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ondansetron alone, taken only as needed

explanation.summary: Highly emetogenic chemotherapy such as cisplatin calls for at least a three-drug regimen: aprepitant, ondansetron, and dexamethasone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cisplatin has the highest emesis risk of the chemotherapy drugs (incidence >90%). A multi-drug regimen is preferred because it blocks stimuli from multiple sources, and such a patient receives at least aprepitant, ondansetron, and dexamethasone. An antimuscarinic or D2 antagonist may be added later if needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This omits the NK1 and 5-HT3 antagonists that form the core of the three-drug regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D2 antagonists and antimuscarinics are add-ons when needed, and ginger is not a substitute for established therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single agent used as needed is inadequate for a highly emetogenic agent; a multi-drug preventive regimen is preferred.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These target motion sickness and pregnancy-associated nausea, not highly emetogenic chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman taking fluoxetine for depression is given high-dose metoclopramide for persistent vomiting. Several hours later she is agitated, tremulous, diaphoretic, and hyperreflexic with a temperature of 38.9 C. Which of the following best explains her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute dystonia from blockade of 5-HT3 receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutropenic fever from bone marrow suppression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serotonin syndrome from the drug combination

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide should not be combined with SSRIs because of the risk of serotonin syndrome, especially in children, young adults, and at high doses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick warns that metoclopramide should not be used with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors because of the risk of serotonin syndrome. The risk is greatest in children and young adults and at high doses, matching this young patient on fluoxetine given a high dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dystonia is a D2-related adverse effect, and it does not explain fever, diaphoresis and hyperreflexia after an SSRI combination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anticholinergic toxicity is caused by antimuscarinics such as scopolamine; metoclopramide does not block muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperglycemia is an adverse effect of steroids such as dexamethasone, not of metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutropenia is an uncommon adverse effect of aprepitant, not of metoclopramide combined with an SSRI.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with diabetic gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for over a year. His wife notices repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and grimacing. The movements continue months after the drug is stopped. Which adverse effect does this most likely represent?

explanation.summary: Long-term metoclopramide can cause tardive dyskinesia, which is often irreversible.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metoclopramide's severe CNS adverse effects include extrapyramidal symptoms, Parkinsonian features, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and tardive dyskinesia. Tardive dyskinesia presents as repetitive involuntary orofacial movements and is often irreversible, which fits movements that persist after stopping the drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergic effects come from antimuscarinics like scopolamine, not metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is an acute, severe reaction rather than slowly developing repetitive orofacial movements that persist after the drug is stopped.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serotonin syndrome is an acute toxicity with the SSRI combination, not a chronic persistent orofacial movement disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Torsades is a ventricular arrhythmia from QT prolongation, not a movement disorder.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man applies a transdermal patch behind his ear before a week-long sailing trip because he becomes nauseated whenever he is on a boat. The drug crosses the blood-brain barrier and prevents signals from the inner ear from triggering nausea. What is its mechanism of action?

explanation.summary: Scopolamine treats motion sickness by blocking central M1 muscarinic receptors in the vestibular nausea pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vestibular system communicates with the nucleus tractus solitarius to induce nausea and vomiting. Scopolamine is a nonspecific muscarinic antagonist that crosses the BBB and blocks the M1 receptor, which treats motion sickness. A transdermal patch reduces its adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: D2 blockade in the area postrema is metoclopramide's mechanism, not that of a motion sickness patch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NK1 blockade is aprepitant's mechanism, used as chemotherapy pre-treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 5-HT3 blockade is the mechanism of ondansetron and related drugs used for chemotherapy-induced nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the proposed antiemetic mechanism of corticosteroids such as dexamethasone.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman uses a scopolamine product for vertigo-associated nausea. Which of the following findings is most likely on her examination?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cool, pale skin with heavy sweating

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dilated pupils and a dry mouth

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinics such as scopolamine cause pupillary dilation, dry mouth, and possible sedation.
explanation.whyCorrect: All anticholinergics have major adverse effects of pupillary dilation, dry mouth, and possible sedation. The mnemonic adds blurry vision, overheating, flushed skin, urinary retention, and confusion. A transdermal patch helps limit these effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Miosis and excess salivation reflect cholinergic excess, the opposite of muscarinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Muscarinic blockade produces hot, dry, flushed skin rather than cool, sweaty skin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These reflect corticosteroid exposure, not an antimuscarinic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antimuscarinics cause urinary retention, not incontinence; bradycardia is a cholinergic effect.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes receives a three-drug pre-treatment regimen before each cycle of cyclophosphamide. Her fingerstick glucose readings are markedly elevated for two days after each infusion. Which component of the regimen is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: When steroids are used for chemotherapy-induced nausea, their most common adverse effects are hyperglycemia and GI bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone are commonly combined with other antiemetics as pre-treatment for chemotherapy. When used this way, the most common adverse effects are hyperglycemia and risk of GI bleed, so a diabetic patient's glucose would rise after each cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aprepitant has few adverse effects; uncommon ones are neutropenia and fatigue, not hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metoclopramide's adverse effects are CNS, extrapyramidal and QT effects, not hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ondansetron causes headache, dizziness, constipation and rarely QT prolongation, not hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Palonosetron is also a 5-HT3 antagonist and is not associated with hyperglycemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has persistent nausea at home between chemotherapy cycles despite taking ondansetron regularly. She takes no other psychiatric or cardiac medications. She wants an additional oral medication with a different mechanism that she can take at home. Which agent is the most appropriate addition?

explanation.summary: For breakthrough nausea at home despite a 5-HT3 antagonist, a D2 antagonist such as metoclopramide adds a different mechanism.
explanation.whyCorrect: D2 antagonists are generally reserved for breakthrough nausea and vomiting when other medications have not provided enough relief. Aprepitant and dexamethasone are used mainly as pre-treatment, and scopolamine is most helpful for motion sickness. Metoclopramide adds D2 blockade to her 5-HT3 blockade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NK1 antagonists are used primarily as pre-treatment before chemotherapy infusions, not for ongoing nausea at home.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Steroids are used primarily as pre-treatment before infusions, not as a home add-on for nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Palonosetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist with the same mechanism as the ondansetron she already takes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antimuscarinics are most helpful for motion sickness, so they are not the best choice here.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man receiving ondansetron with each chemotherapy cycle reports a new adverse effect after starting it. Which of the following is a common adverse effect of this drug?

explanation.summary: Common adverse effects of 5-HT3 antagonists are headache, dizziness, and constipation; QT prolongation is rare but major.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ondansetron and the other 5-HT3 antagonists commonly cause headache, dizziness, and constipation. A major but rare adverse effect is prolongation of the QT interval.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperglycemia is a common adverse effect of steroids such as dexamethasone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactation results from metoclopramide's removal of dopamine's inhibition of prolactin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tardive dyskinesia is a CNS adverse effect of the D2 antagonist metoclopramide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary retention is an anticholinergic adverse effect of antimuscarinics such as scopolamine.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has daily nausea and vomiting. Dietary changes and ginger have not been enough. Which of the following is an established pharmacologic treatment with good evidence for her condition?

explanation.summary: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6), alone or with doxylamine, has well-established evidence for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy; the combination is an established pharmacologic treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ginger and pyridoxine have the strongest evidence for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. Pyridoxine can be used alone or with doxylamine, and the doxylamine-pyridoxine combination is an established pharmacologic treatment rather than a dietary supplement alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These are pre-treatment agents for chemotherapy-induced nausea, not therapy for nausea of pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Evidence for chamomile and peppermint is substantially weaker and does not support routine use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These have only limited or emerging evidence and are not established antiemetic therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These target motion sickness and breakthrough chemotherapy nausea; neither is the established treatment for nausea of pregnancy described here.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis takes an over-the-counter H1 antihistamine and notices that her runny nose improves. This symptom relief is most directly explained by which of the following actions of the drug on endothelial cells adjacent to vascular smooth muscle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of mast cell degranulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of nitric oxide and prostacyclin release

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines reduce nasal symptoms by blocking H1 receptors, which inhibits nitric oxide and prostacyclin release and produces vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: By antagonizing H1 receptors on endothelial cells, the drug inhibits the release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin. This causes vasoconstriction and reduces edema formation, lessening runny nose symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H1 antihistamines act on histamine receptors, not nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking gastric acid secretion is a function of H2 blockers, not H1 antihistamines used for allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor; they do not trigger mast cell degranulation, which is what releases histamine in the first place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased nitric oxide and prostacyclin would cause vasodilation and worsen edema, the opposite of the drug's effect.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man takes diphenhydramine for allergies and becomes very drowsy, while his coworker taking loratadine for the same allergies reports no sedation. Which property of diphenhydramine best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is hydrophilic and cannot enter the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: It selectively blocks H2 receptors in the stomach

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier, blocking central H1 receptors and causing sedation.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines are lipophilic and readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so they block central H1 receptors that normally promote wakefulness, producing drowsiness. Second-generation drugs like loratadine are hydrophilic and penetrate the brain poorly, so they are non-sedating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation, not a second-generation, antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is lipophilic, not hydrophilic; that is precisely why it enters the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diphenhydramine blocks H1, not H2 receptors, and H2 blockade would not explain sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug blocks H1 receptors; it does not stimulate central histamine release.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed a non-sedating antihistamine for chronic urticaria so that daytime alertness is preserved. Which of the following agents best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines such as fexofenadine are non-sedating because they poorly cross the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine. These agents are hydrophilic, act primarily on peripheral H1 receptors, and cause little sedation, making them ideal when alertness must be preserved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation agent that crosses the blood-brain barrier and can cause sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is a lipophilic first-generation agent that causes marked drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine and is sedating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Promethazine is a first-generation agent with sedating and antimuscarinic properties.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is brought in for confusion, blurred vision, dry mouth, and difficulty urinating that began after he started an over-the-counter first-generation antihistamine. These findings are best explained by the drug's action at which of the following receptors?

explanation.summary: Many first-generation antihistamines also block muscarinic receptors, producing anticholinergic side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines have antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) activity. Blockade of muscarinic receptors causes dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, and, especially in the elderly, confusion and delirium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2 blockade relates to bronchial and vascular tone, not dry mouth and urinary retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal effects, not the dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2 receptors regulate gastric acid; blocking them does not cause this anticholinergic toxidrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic receptor blockade would affect the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, not this pattern of anticholinergic findings.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has persistent nausea and vomiting. Her physician prescribes doxylamine in combination with which of the following, an FDA-approved regimen for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?

explanation.summary: Doxylamine plus vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is an approved treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that doxylamine, a first-generation antihistamine, combined with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), is approved for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. First-generation agents cross the placenta but are unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects but is not the antiemetic partner of doxylamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 is used for pernicious anemia, not paired with doxylamine for pregnancy nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin C is not part of this regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D addresses bone and calcium metabolism, not nausea of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A family planning a road trip asks for a medication to prevent motion sickness in an adult. Which antihistamine is most appropriate, and what property makes it effective for this indication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cetirizine, because it is hydrophilic and non-sedating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desloratadine, because it blocks H2 receptors in the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fexofenadine, because it acts only at peripheral sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loratadine, because it is non-sedating and long acting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promethazine, because of its antimuscarinic properties

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines with antimuscarinic activity, such as promethazine, are effective against motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that first-generation antihistamines like promethazine and dimenhydrinate have antimuscarinic properties that make them effective in treating motion sickness. Second-generation agents lack this activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cetirizine is a second-generation agent lacking meaningful antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desloratadine is an H1, not H2, agent and is second-generation; it is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fexofenadine acts only peripherally and is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loratadine is a peripherally acting second-generation agent without the antimuscarinic activity needed for motion sickness.

questions.stem: In a review of histamine physiology, a student notes where the H1 receptor is located relative to other histamine receptor subtypes. According to the brick, where are H2 histamine receptors primarily located?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems

explanation.summary: H2 histamine receptors are found primarily in gastric cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that H2 histamine receptors are primarily in gastric cells, H3 receptors in the neurons, and H4 receptors in the bone marrow, whereas H1 receptors are widespread and are the target of antihistamine therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The bone marrow is the location of H4, not H2, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The neurons are where H3 receptors are located.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vascular endothelial cells express the H1 receptors targeted by antihistamines, not H2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Widespread distribution in the central and peripheral nervous systems describes H1 receptors.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is given a first-generation antihistamine and, instead of becoming sleepy, develops restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia. This response is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sign of H2 receptor blockade

choices.label: C
choices.text: A withdrawal effect from stopping the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: An allergic reaction to the drug

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines can cause paradoxical CNS stimulation in children younger than about six years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick warns that in children younger than six, first-generation antihistamines can, at regular doses, cause a paradoxical CNS stimulation manifesting as restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia rather than the usual drowsiness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These first-generation agents act at H1 and muscarinic receptors, not H2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The reaction occurred after taking the drug, not after stopping it, so it is not withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The symptoms are a CNS drug effect, not an allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The child is stimulated, not sedated, so this is not the expected sedative effect.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine for seasonal allergies. Through its anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) action, this drug is most likely to produce which of the following effects in the eye?

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinic action at the eye causes pupil dilation and reduced tear formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 2 lists the ocular anticholinergic effects as mydriasis (dilation) and decreased lacrimation, which clinically produce blurred vision and dry eyes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antimuscarinic effects decrease, not increase, intestinal motility, causing constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antimuscarinic activity decreases sweating rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antimuscarinic activity decreases urination, causing retention, not increased output.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Miosis and increased tears are cholinergic effects, the opposite of antimuscarinic blockade.

questions.stem: A patient taking a second-generation antihistamine for allergies reports only a mild headache and occasional fatigue, with no significant dry mouth or drowsiness. This favorable side-effect profile compared with first-generation agents is best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced release of histamine from mast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Greater lipophilicity and stronger blood-brain barrier penetration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible binding to H1 receptors in the brain

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines penetrate the brain poorly and have little antimuscarinic activity, so side effects are mild and non-specific.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because second-generation agents are hydrophilic and act mainly on peripheral H1 receptors, they cause much less sedation and few antimuscarinic effects. Their adverse effects are usually mild and non-specific, such as headache, diarrhea, or fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor and do not enhance histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Greater lipophilicity and brain penetration would increase, not decrease, sedation, and describes first-generation agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 antihistamines are competitive (reversible) H1 blockers, not irreversible binders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These drugs block H1 receptors; nicotinic blockade is not their mechanism.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man reports several weeks of new daytime sleepiness. Medication review reveals he recently added an over-the-counter pill containing diphenhydramine to help him sleep. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to address his sleepiness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a second-generation antihistamine on top of the diphenhydramine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add an H2 blocker to counteract the sedation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to promethazine for its antimuscarinic effect

explanation.summary: Sedation from a first-generation antihistamine is managed by stopping the offending drug and substituting a non-sedating agent if needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case, the patient's new sleepiness is caused by diphenhydramine, a sedating first-generation antihistamine. The remedy is to stop that drug and, if antihistamine therapy is still needed, replace it with a non-sedating second-generation agent such as loratadine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding another antihistamine keeps the sedating diphenhydramine on board and does not fix the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An H2 blocker treats gastric acid and would not counteract the sedation from an H1 agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing the dose of the sedating drug would worsen the sleepiness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Promethazine is another sedating first-generation agent and would not relieve the drowsiness.

questions.stem: H1 antihistamines are best classified pharmacologically as which of the following with respect to the H1 receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competitive antagonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Full agonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective agonists at H2 and H3 receptors

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines act by competitively binding to H1 receptors as antagonists or inverse agonists.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes H1 antihistamines as histamine antagonists and inverse agonists that work by competitively binding to H1 receptors, thereby blocking histamine's effects.

whyWrongByChoice.B: They are receptor blockers, not enzymes that degrade histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They oppose, rather than activate, the H1 receptor, so they are not full agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They block the receptor; they do not inhibit histamine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They target the H1 receptor and are not agonists at H2 or H3 receptors.
